branch: ب ص ر usage ↔ ث ب ت B006
after: The ruin sites function as evidence placed before the discerning mind.
reason: The focus says the dwellings have become clear to the audience, and those remains can function as evidence that supports knowing. The proof branch is a useful neighboring idea, though it describes what produces insight rather than the participle's own sense.

after: Their former homes can be heard as terrain still within sight.
reason: The sight-range land branch finds a faint setting in `مَسَٰكِنِهِمْ`: the remains are dwelling terrain exposed to view, while `تَّبَيَّنَ` makes them evident. The verse gives no explicit eye or boundary of vision, so this remains a landscape echo.

after: The bodily sense of seeing shadows the question about whether they saw creation.
reason: In 29:19, `يَرَوْا۟` asks whether people see how creation begins, which can make the closing participle retain an outward visual edge. Since the verb also allows reflective consideration, it only weakly singles out bodily sight.

after: The ending can also suggest people equipped to look, against the surah's command to inspect the earth.
reason: The command `فَٱنظُرُوا۟` explicitly directs the audience to look after traveling across the earth, activating the bodily seeing branch beside `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ`. The ruined dwellings made clear in 29:38 then give that looking a concrete object, so perception can be heard as sight as well as understanding.

after: The bodily sight sense acquires a shadow of blindness after refusal.
reason: The phrase `فَعَمُوا۟` names blindness and supplies an opposite image for the seeing sense in the focus participle. The other verse may mean spiritual blindness, so this does not make the people in 29:38 physically blind; it is a contrastive echo.

after: A straight path is set beside a possible loss of sight.
reason: Fatiha's `ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ` names the straight path, while the proposed eye branch describes a sound pupil with sight gone. Read against 29:38, where people with perception are turned from `ٱلسَّبِيلِ`, the pairing hints that correct direction and clear sight can come apart, but the eye loss is not stated.

after: Fatiha's bestowed favor can faintly call the eye's delight idiom.
reason: The dictionary's eye-delight idiom can be heard beside `أَنْعَمْتَ`, the act of bestowing favor in Fatiha. The link adds a possible sense of seeing as delight, but neither the focus nor that clause names the eye or joy directly.

after: The sinking earth faintly recalls sight drawn inward and lost.
reason: The bridge joins a dictionary image of an eye that has lost sight with `خَسَفْنَا بِهِ ٱلْأَرْضَ`, the earth swallowing one group. That concrete sinking can call the related image of a pupil receding, though no human eye is mentioned in the punishment scene.

after: Their inward understanding is set against clarity that has already emerged from the ruins.
reason: The clause `قَد تَّبَيَّنَ لَكُم مِّن مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ` says the evidence from their dwellings has become clear, directly calling the branch of inward apprehension. Its placement before `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ` makes public clarity and the former peoples' capacity to understand one joined image.

after: Their discernment stands beside deeds that were made attractive to them.
reason: `وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ ٱلشَّيْطَٰنُ أَعْمَٰلَهُمْ` supplies an actual act of beautifying that can distort inward judgment. The contrast lets `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ` suggest that they possessed discernment while being drawn by a false appearance, rather than changing its basic sense to beauty.

after: Human discernment is framed near the surah's later naming of divine wisdom.
reason: The focus describes human beings as capable of inward perception, and the same surah later closes a statement about God's knowledge with `ٱلْعَزِيزُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ`. The wisdom term makes the cognitive branch concrete while sharpening the contrast between the peoples' capacity and their misdirection.

after: The word for reprehensible things faintly calls the boundary of recognition.
reason: The branch includes failing to recognize or acknowledge what is known, and `وَٱلْمُنكَرِ` supplies a local word from that recognition field. In 29:45 it means wrongdoing, so the cognitive sense is only a secondary resonance beside its moral meaning.

after: The focus's insight is echoed by the audience who can reason from a surviving sign.
reason: At 29:35, the surah says it left a clear sign `لِّقَوْمٍ يَعْقِلُونَ`, naming the very capacity to reason that the B002 branch describes. The shared thread is understanding evidence, so the later description `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ` gains a sharper, potentially ironic tie to people who had that capacity yet followed a wrong path.

after: The surah links inward apprehension with a command to examine creation.
reason: The command `فَٱنظُرُوا۟ كَيْفَ بَدَأَ ٱلْخَلْقَ` asks travelers to inspect how creation began, activating directed reflection rather than bare eyesight alone. Beside `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ`, that command makes insight an exercised way of reaching understanding from signs.

after: The rhetorical question about seeing creation also presses toward a considered judgment.
reason: In 29:19, `أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا۟ كَيْفَ يُبْدِئُ ٱللَّهُ ٱلْخَلْقَ` can mean more than receiving an image: it calls the audience to reflect on what creation shows. That thinking sense of seeing activates inward discernment alongside the focus participle's insight sense.

after: The spider-house parable ends with a question of whether its audience knows.
reason: The concept path from wisdom through ignorance reaches `لَوْ كَانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ`, an explicit knowing phrase after the spider's fragile house. This repeats the surah's concern with understanding, but it is a broad cognitive echo rather than a distinct new image for the focus word.

after: The peoples' capacity for discernment is cast against hearts that became blind.
reason: The other ayah says `فَعَمُوا۟` after people turn away, an explicit image of blindness that can describe lost inward discernment. Set beside `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ`, it makes the focus's inner-sight branch audible as the opposite capacity, while 29:38 itself narrates how attractive deeds still divert them.

after: The plea for guidance on the straight path completes the focus's insight-and-diversion contrast.
reason: Fatiha's `ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَٰطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ` joins guidance to a right way, while 29:38 says Satan turned the people `عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ`. That shared path language gives inward discernment a directional consequence: insight is bound to finding and keeping the way.

after: The people are described against a sign that has already become clear to its audience.
reason: This branch includes a sign that makes people able to see or understand, and `قَد تَّبَيَّنَ لَكُم مِّن مَّسَٰكِنِهِمْ` immediately supplies that illuminating clarification. The focus participle `مُسْتَبْصِرِينَ` then names people able to perceive, so the root can shadow a quality of the sign as well as a quality of its audience.

after: The written book can faintly suggest an assembled whole with joined parts.
reason: The seam-and-joining branch has a weak conceptual cue in `ٱلْكِتَٰبِ`, a book that gathers written parts into one object. Nothing in 29:45 mentions stitching, skins, or a thick edge, so the physical join remains only a note beside the scriptural sense.

after: The punishment by a stone shower offers a rough echo of the stone branch.
reason: The concept chain reaches `حَاصِبًا`, a punishment image involving stones, which supplies a real stone trigger for the soft-stone branch. The verse does not call the stones soft, pale, or shiny, so only the broad material category is activated.
